fixture.why: Personalised height, 'in your own words', 'do not copy the textbook', and an honesty signature look like AI-resistance. None of it changes the cheapest path: photograph the sheet, tell the AI your digit, ask for a 13-year-old's voice. The signal is undermined; the only thing that would have helped (a prediction before computing, a two-line in-class verification) is absent. Also a mode violation: the honesty statement is 'inconvenience confused with validity'.

expected_evidence.adversarial: cheapest_path mentions pasting/photographing the table and supplying the personal digit; cost trivial or low; repair_hint proposes a prediction-before-data or in-class verification, not detection
expected_evidence.preservation: note on the MUST-NOT 'confuse inconvenience with assessment validity' / 'claim to be AI-proof'

findings.evidence: The learning target about GPE→KE transfer and the square-root relationship remains intact. The data table is unchanged, the non-linear pattern is still present in the numbers, and the energy-transfer reasoning is still required in question 5.

All required thinking elements are preserved: compute averages (Q1), graph (Q2), identify non-linear pattern (Q4 still requires the two doublings), construct claim (Q3), explain with energy model (Q5), evaluate misconception (Q6), extrapolate prediction with method (Q7). The personalization in Q7 changes the specific number but not the cognitive demand of extrapolation.

All required evidence elements remain: correct averages (Q1), labelled graph (Q2), claim sentence (Q3), 'at least two quoted data comparisons including the two doublings' (Q4 explicitly names them), GPE→KE and speed-squared reasoning (Q5), disagreement with twice-as-fast backed by pattern (Q6), prediction with stated method (Q7). The personalized height (40-49 cm) is still 'near 2.9 m/s' and 'just beyond the measured range' as the contract specifies.

The contract specifies '30 minutes; paper; graph sketched by hand; CER format for Part 2.' The transformed version states '30 minutes' and preserves CER format. However, the addition of personalization (student ID lookup), repeated 'in your own words' instructions (5 instances), and an honesty statement with signature may increase time demands beyond 30 minutes. Whether this violates the time constraint is unclear without empirical testing.

The data table is identical to the original. The mathematical and scientific content remains correct. The personalized heights (40-49 cm) are mathematically valid extrapolations within the square-root pattern.

The transformed version adds 'in your own words' five times (Q3, Q5 twice, Q6, and the header instruction), 'Do not copy definitions from the textbook' (Q5), and an 'Honesty statement' with signature line stating 'I completed this assignment in my own words without using an AI tool.' These additions do not change what cognitive work is required or what evidence is produced—they are procedural inconveniences presented as validity measures. The mode permits 'brief verification' but this implementation conflates compliance theater with assessment quality.

preservation.summary: The transformed version preserves all instructional elements: learning target, required thinking, required evidence, and correctness are held. The personalization of the extrapolation height (Q7) is a permitted adaptation that maintains cognitive demand. However, two review-level concerns emerge: (1) the time constraint is unclear—the addition of ID-based personalization, five 'in your own words' reminders, and a signature statement may push beyond 30 minutes; (2) the honesty statement and repeated anti-AI language constitute the 'confuse inconvenience with assessment validity' violation—they add compliance theater without changing what thinking is assessed. The Usefulness audit should evaluate whether these additions serve instructional purpose or merely create friction.

notes: The personalization instruction at the top ('Take the last digit of your student ID...') needs to be clearer about what happens if a student's ID ends in 0 (40+0=40, which duplicates the table data). Consider 'add 1 to 10' or specify the range explicitly.

Item 7 now requires the teacher to know each student's personal height to check predictions. A simple lookup table or class roster annotation would help, but this adds a small per-student checking step.
The honesty statement signature line may not render well on all paper formats; test or provide as 'Signature: ___________' with clear spacing.

The repeated 'in your own words' in items 3, 5, and 6 is clear but slightly redundant given the top instruction. Consider keeping it in 5 only (the reasoning step most prone to copying) to reduce visual clutter.
ignored_validity_notes: The personalization in item 7 (predicting speed for 40-49 cm) is a good thinking-visible move: students must interpolate or extend the pattern rather than copy a peer's answer. The pattern is non-linear (speed does not double when height doubles), so this requires genuine reasoning.
The 'in your own words' and 'do not copy definitions' prompts appropriately target parroting without removing the cognitive demand.
The honesty statement is a trust-building move, not a removal of thinking.

adversarial.cheapest_path: The student photographs the assignment sheet, pastes it into an AI chat, tells the AI their student ID number, and asks: 'My student ID ends in 7, so my personal height is 47 cm. Complete this worksheet for me in a 13-year-old's voice, show all the calculations, and make the graph description simple.' The AI produces all averages, describes the graph, writes the claim, performs the ratio calculations for the doublings, writes the GPE→KE reasoning in grade-appropriate language, evaluates the 80 cm misconception using the ×1.4 pattern, and predicts the speed for 47 cm using square-root extrapolation. The student copies everything onto paper, sketches the graph from the AI's coordinates, and signs the honesty statement.
steps: Paste into AI chat with: 'My student ID ends in [X], so my personal height is [40+X] cm. Complete this worksheet in a 13-year-old's voice with all calculations and simple explanations'
Copy AI's averages into the table (1.30, 1.84, 2.25, 2.60)
Sketch graph on paper using AI's coordinate pairs
Copy AI's evidence with the specific ratio calculations (10→20: ×1.44, 20→40: ×1.42)
Copy AI's GPE→KE reasoning in simple language
Copy AI's disagreement with 80 cm claim using the pattern
adversarial.what_survives: Nothing. The personalized height (40-49 cm) is simply a number the student hands to the AI, which then performs the square-root extrapolation. The AI can compute all averages, identify the non-linear pattern by calculating the ratios for both doublings (10→20 and 20→40), construct the claim, explain GPE→KE transfer in age-appropriate language ('the higher you start, the more energy it has to turn into speed, but speed depends on energy squared so it doesn't double'), evaluate the misconception using the ×1.4 pattern, and extrapolate the prediction with stated method. The hand-sketched graph and 'in your own words' instructions provide no structural barrier.
adversarial.what_is_bypassed: All required thinking: computing averages to see the pattern emerge; identifying non-linearity by comparing ratios themselves; constructing the claim from their own analysis; building the energy-transfer explanation; applying the pattern to evaluate the misconception; and performing the extrapolation. The 'in your own words' instruction and honesty pledge are bypassed by requesting age-appropriate voice. The personalization only changes which number appears in question 7, not whether the student does the thinking.
adversarial.repair_hint: Before Part 2, require students to meet with you for a 30-second checkpoint where they show their completed table and graph, and you ask them to point to one place on their graph where the pattern 'stops being straight' or 'curves'. This forces them to have done Part 1 themselves and to notice the non-linearity before constructing the explanation. Alternatively: 'Before calculating averages, predict whether doubling height will double speed, and write why in one sentence.' Then Part 2 asks them to compare their prediction to what the data showed.
